newsitem.title: UK: NSea Brent dips on ample avails, closed U.S. arb.
newsitem.headline: NSea Brent dips on ample avails, closed U.S. arb.

text.p: North Sea Brent crude took another dip on the physical market on Monday, with traders saying the fall was due to ample June avails and closed arbitrage to the United States.

A June 11-13 loader was sold by one trading house to another at July Brent -37 cents and a second cargo (June 12-14) fetched the same price or seven cents lower than a June 16-18 sold at a 30 cents discount to July Brent.
"There's some cargoes around, still unsold, and the arbitrage to the United States is closed," the seller said, commenting on the distressed price that the cargo fetched.

On cash, it was a different picture as July Brent was trading 12 cents a barrel up, at $19.52 by 1731 GMT. London crude futures rose on the back of a stronger-than expected technical picture for NYMEX crude and products.
Earlier, July Brent fetched $19.41 a barrel on the paper market, a cent up on Friday's London close but 10 cents weaker than a handful of trades in the after-hours U.S. market.
Prompt Brent intermonth spreads weakened further, with Jun/Jul talked at -18/-14 cents, or some four cents weaker from earlier talk and after trading at -12 cents late Friday.
Jul/Aug was fairly steady at -13/-10 cents.

Brent Contracts for Differences also eased further, with this week talked at July Brent -39/-35 cents after trading earlier at a 33 cents discount to July Brent. Next week's CFDs (June 9-13) also slipped some four cents to July Brent -36/-32 cents in thin late talk.
Other North Sea grades were on the upside, with an Ekofisk loading June 18-20 sold by a Norwegian producer at Dated Brent +20 cents, three cents higher than a similar cargo done on Friday.
A second Ekofisk loading June 24 was bought by a European refiner at Dated Brent +17 cents.
The Norwegian producer said it was also offering end June Statfjord at Dated Brent +35 cents, two cents up on the last deal for a first decade June done last week.
"There's no first or second decade (June) cargoes left except for one June 18 Statfjord, so that is good," the producer said.

The two Brent cargoes turning wet on Monday were kept ahead of the five o'clock deadline by Morgan Stanley and Koch, traders said. Both cargoes are due to load June 17-19 and one of them was a deferral from Friday.
On the West African market, remaining June barrels were offered at steady levels, with most expected to find homes in the U.S. Gulf.
Two third decade Bonny Light/Bonny Medium combos and two Escravos were expected to be loaded into VLCCs for transatlantic sailing.
At least one of two third decade Qua Iboes were thought already placed into the U.S. Gulf refining belt.
In addition, a third Forcados was offered at Dated Brent +27 cents and a Brass River at Dated Brent +58 cents.
Details of the Nigerian July loading programme were emerging in "dribs and drabs" while the full programme was expected to be released by mid-week.
Traders said that despite a widening Brent/Dubai spread and a sloppy Far eastern market, buying interest in early July barrels was seen from Asian refiners.
"We should see some buying if the (Brent/Dubai spread) stays below a dollar," a trader said.
In the Mediterranean, two large and four small first decade Urals cargoes were on offer at around Dated Brent -$1.35.
Although the main Russian port of Novorossiisk was operating normally after a spill last week, loadings were running about two days behind.
Sour crude buyers were still waiting to hear whether the U.N.-Iraq oil-for-food deal would be renewed after the first six-month period expires on June 7.
"We are still waiting to hear, but I'm very positive that it will happen," said one Med refiner.
U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan on Monday recommended to the Security Council that the deal should be renewed to allow another six-months of oil sales to the value of $2 billion.
-H. Haddadin, R. Russell, London newsroom +44 171 542 8145
